correctness.rationale: Normalized Weyl matrices are an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert–Schmidt space; the orbit phases are distinct orthogonal characters of the N²-element phase space, giving eigenvalue N times the sum of the two squared ambiguities (N=q²). For a nonzero displacement (a,b) the first graph has one overlap iff a≠0, since b=2at−a²; the other has one iff b≠0. At zero displacement a nontrivial quadratic phase has squared sum q by expanding the square and summing in the difference variable; a nontrivial linear phase has zero sum. Thus the five distinct eigenvalues are 1,2,q,2q,2q² with the stated multiplicities, which partition all q⁴ Weyl labels. Minimum and maximum are attained, and their square-root ratio is √2 q. The first window's nonzero labels count q²q(q−1)+q(q−1)+1; the second is symmetric. Any ≤q-point support misses a nonzero difference because 1+q(q−1)<q², leaving a whole Weyl shift sector unseen by that window. This is a linear-matrix statement; injectivity on rank-one projectors follows for the pair but the obstruction for a single window is not asserted in that restricted problem. A fresh finite-field enumeration gave {1:1296,2:5184,9:16,18:64,162:1} for q=9; a separate dense lifted normal matrix gave {1:36,2:36,3:4,6:4,18:1} for q=3. value.rationale: Linear tomography using extremely sparse windows needs both identifiability and stable inversion. This explicit construction attains the minimum possible number of windows under a natural per-window support cap and gives all singular levels, not just full rank. It supplies a precisely conditioned deterministic design over every odd prime power, without making claims about globally best conditioning or pure-state minimality.
